title: The New Industrialists | How AI and Human Ingenuity Are Transforming Industry
transcriptText:
(upbeat music)
- Welcome to The Industrialists,
a video series that explores
the edge of innovation
for manufacturing, mobility, and energy.
I am Adam Bogobowicz, and
I'll be your host and guest
and will walk you through
story, strategies,
and breakthroughs that are
shaping our industrial world.
In this series, we're gonna sit down
with amazing people driving this change.
We're gonna uncover what's
new, what's changing,
what's reshaping how we
should think about building,
moving, and powering the future.
Today, I am on a floor of
Singapore Expo at ITAP,
an amazing show, and I'm
joined here with Uli Homann.
Uli is a distinguished
engineer and CVP at Microsoft.
And Uli is the person
who shaped the concept
of frontier manufacturing.
Uli, thank you for being here
and welcome to The Industrialist.
- Adam, thanks for inviting me.
It's really a pleasure to be
here at this exciting place,
in this exciting venue.
- Uli, so let me start
with this broad concept
of frontier manufacturing.
It's new, we haven't talked about it yet.
What is it? How should we think about it?
- So in general, frontier
company means for us at Microsoft
and now in the industry at large
that you merge human
ingenuity, human creativity,
human risk management
with AI resources
as a single pool of execution
capability for a company.
And you compose people
and AI, specifically agentic AI,
into an execution force that
allows you to achieve outcomes
that previously were very hard to achieve.
And for industrial, it means
that you're now introducing AI
throughout the entire value chain,
from digital engineering
to digital operations
to supply chain management and so forth,
and are really bringing together the best
of what people can do
and the best of what AI can do.
- We've done this before,
we've done automation for
the last decade or two.
How is this thing different?
- This thing is very, very different
in the sense of automation as
we have traditionally done it
relies on software developers
understanding the scenario,
thinking through every possible issue,
every possible scenario,
and then making the decisions
of what to do with a specific event,
with a specific temperature
drop, whatever it might be,
and making the decision
of how the software
is supposed to automate and react.
That's wonderful, but we
don't know everything upfront,
and therefore automation
is always limited.
With AI, what we are seeing
is that we are getting
into a software environment
that is capable of
reasoning over requests,
supported by knowledge.
So any company here in this
environment has knowledge,
has data, that effectively
describes what they do,
how they do it, their proven practices,
their mistakes they
made, and other things.
All of that knowledge packed together
is now being fed to the software system,
which we call agentic AI.
And the AI system has
these language models
like Open AI and Anthropic
and other capabilities
to reason over
that knowledge based
upon the input they get,
in event like the temperature has dropped
for a specific part.
And instead of having
predefined software code paths,
you effectively have a system
that now intelligently looks at it
and makes a decision and
creates a plan for execution.
You then add tools to it,
meaning a software agent is like a brain,
it knows how to react to things,
but it needs an arm and a
leg to do certain things,
and the agent will call
those things tools,
and I can now press an alarm button
or stop the production line
or whatever the right action might be.
And that's really the difference.
So we will get to a much
higher degree of automation
because the software
doesn't have to be prebuilt
to think about everything
that might happen.
- So I see this is about data
and about technology and infrastructure.
Is it also about people?
- Absolutely.
As I said before, people
are the key ingredient.
AI is the supporting team
and the people are actually,
to use an American football
term, the quarterbacks,
they define what play we
go and why we do this play,
and the AI team is effectively the system
that executes the how,
how are we going to do it?
But before we get to a how,
we have to know why we're
doing certain things
and what we are going to do.
And that's really the job of people.
So together, that really makes
the frontier company work.
- I love the human component of it,
that everything is changing
and we gotta change with it.
But what's enabling this?
What's fundamental to enabling
the system to actually work?
- Yeah, so the way I think about this
is it all comes down to data,
data that is accessible to the AI system.
We call it knowledge in the AI language.
Effectively enabled software systems
that are now based on AI to
make intelligent decisions.
That's already fantastic.
But what we also need to do,
and that's the second half of
the coin, or the second side,
is really thinking about governance
because with great power
comes great responsibility,
as Mr. Spider-Man said.
And so my view is, as a company,
you need to invest in
making the data accessible,
make it available,
but then also invest in
observability and governance
so that at any point in time
throughout the execution of the AI agents,
the guardrails that we set up as people,
the what and the why,
are executed
And if the AI system gets
something wrong, which can happen,
we have the power and ability
to stop the system at any
point in time, reset it,
and start the process again.
And that's really the two halves
that I believe are critical.
And then as a person,
you have to start to
learn how to be a CEO,
because ultimately, you will have a team
of agents that work for you.
You are the supervisor of these agents,
you have to direct them,
you have to guide them,
you are setting the guardrails
of how these agents execute.
And that means all of us
have to start to think about,
can I direct agents to an
outcome that makes sense?
- So let me pull on this thread,
because enterprise is complicated,
manufacturing is complicated.
It's not just generic agents,
it's also about agents in specific places.
Does it look differently in
operations than in engineering?
What is the difference between
this future agentic digital operations
and digital engineering?
- From a technology perspective,
there is very little difference,
because we're doing the same thing.
However, the agents are A,
drawing on different knowledge.
So in the operational side,
you would worry about OEEs,
you're worried about efficiency,
you're worrying about
inventory getting too low
or changes in the production line,
weather changes, whatever it might be.
And therefore the agent has
to have a different knowledge base,
and obviously it has
to have different tools
that it can access to affect outcome.
- Yep.
- If you go
to the digital engineering side,
it starts off with, okay,
what is the market situation?
Where do we are competitive?
Where are we not competitive?
So the sources of knowhow for
the agent are very different,
and that's really the big difference.
And then the tools that
are affecting the outcome.
For example, in manufacturing,
you're dealing with real
robots, with real hardware.
In the engineering side,
you're dealing with software,
with simulation, with other tools
that are not affecting
the physical outcome,
but are preparing for
the physical outcome.
- So let me pull on this one.
I like the robotics component
of what you're saying,
because that's the physical manifestation
that today is light on AI.
Are the robots going to change
because we now build models
and GenAI that we can
interact with those robots?
- Yes, of course.
So this is going to happen very quick.
What did I read?
By 2030, 70% of the industry people
think that robots, intelligent robots,
will enter the manufacturing environment.
And again, the key thing
is that the robot will look
at the tool and the task
and make decisions intelligently.
So it's not just simply executing
a script, one, two, three,
It will look at the part, for example,
and if it's not correctly
positioned for manufacturing,
it will automatically
adjust, like a human would.
And so it deals with uncertainty
and with non-precision
much differently than
traditional automation.
And that's why the robots
and intelligence will come together.
- So now let's think about,
and take it from a perspective
of somebody running a
manufacturing operations today,
engineering and manufacturing operations,
this wave of innovation is coming in,
we're all trying to adjust it,
we even see this vision
of frontier firm as the
way to think about it.
But what are the fundamental capabilities
that somebody would need to
build, not only the future,
but today, to be able to take
advantage of this opportunity?
- Well, you should listen
to Mike later in the conversation,
but ultimately what it really
means is you have to start
to connect all of your assets.
You have to find a operation center
where all of the data from
your assets come together,
then being analyzed and
intelligently looked at
to define the knowledge and the recipe,
and then you drive the
automation in a closed loop.
And this dream has been around forever,
but because of the way of standards
like OPC UA and others
enabling us to take to any
machine out there, or any asset,
bringing it together
into cloud environments
with modern connectivity
and the scale of processing
in terms of data management
and development of AI solutions,
and then the automation
against the assets that we have
is now much, much easier
and much more reasonable
from a cost efficiency
and effort perspective
than ever before.
Is it easy? No.
But is it easier than even
five years ago? Absolutely.
And again, we normally don't talk
much about products in this talk,
but Azure IoT operations
is that breakthrough
that we have been building
to build on top of standards,
bringing assets into a management
and data analytics environment
that is modern, scalable,
and effectively enables you
to drive this closed loop,
together with partners,
because Microsoft is an
enabling technology set,
and partners from Siemens
to Schneider to Rockwell
to ABB and others
are working together with us to figure out
how we make this dream reality.
- Uli, thank you so much.
Thank you for being here.
Thank you for joining
us at The Industrialist.
If this conversation sparked
questions or thoughts,
please share it with us.
I'm Adam Bogobowicz,
and I'll be back with more stories
about the future of technology
in the industrial space.
(upbeat music)
